Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) shares fell 2.01% to $28.02 as of 11:05 a.m. ET in regular trading on November 10, as AI hardware names cooled after a hotter-than-expected October CPI report. The server maker issued no company-specific news today.

The latest numbers explain the market's caution. Fiscal first-quarter revenue reached $19.9 billion, nearly four times the $5.0 billion of a year earlier, and diluted EPS rose to $1.75. Operating cash flow was negative $434 million, as receivables and inventory absorbed about $6 billion, partly offset by customer deposits. Gross margin fell to 12.7% from 17.5% in the prior quarter. title: Super Micro Earned $1.6 Billion Last Quarter. Slight Problem: Its Operating Cash Flow Was Negative $434 Million

Super Micro Earned $1.6 Billion Last Quarter. Slight Problem: Its Operating Cash Flow Was Negative $434 Million
Gian Estrada

Trade SMCI on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Super Micro Earned $1.6 Billion Last Quarter. Slight Problem: Its Operating Cash Flow Was Negative $434 Million ©@Cnv Studio from CnvStudio's Images via Canva, @primeimages from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Super Micro's revenue nearly quadrupled to $19.9 billion in the September quarter and it earned $1.6 billion, but operating cash flow was negative $434 million.

The cash went into receivables and inventory, and about $3.1 billion of customer prepayments kept the outflow from being far larger.

At 4.7x forward earnings, the stock is priced as if the cash never comes, and the December quarter is the next test.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) just had the biggest quarter in its history. In the three months to Sept. 30, revenue nearly quadrupled to $19.9 billion, and net income jumped to $1.59 billion from $168 million, according to its preliminary results.

That was more than $4 billion above the original guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. But Super Micro had already raised the range on Oct. 20, and the stock fell 11% in the week into the Nov. 3 report.

Where the Profit Went

The profit hasn't turned into cash because the build-out absorbed it. Receivables rose $3.6 billion, and inventory climbed to $15.1 billion from $12.9 billion at the end of June.

Deferred revenue rose about $3.1 billion, an "overwhelming majority" of which reflects customers paying ahead of delivery, new CFO Mark Long said on his first call. Without those prepayments, the quarter's operating outflow would have been closer to $3.5 billion.

Analysts expect free cash flow to swing from negative $7.0 billion in fiscal 2026, the year to June, to positive $4.0 billion in fiscal 2027:

SMCI Free Cash Flow Estimates: FY2024-FY2029 (TIKR)

After negative $476 million in the first quarter, the next three need to bring in about $4.5 billion between them. That's a lot to ask of a company still growing this fast.

Growth Is Eating Super Micro's Cash

Nothing in the quarter suggests customers are slow to pay. Days sales outstanding fell to 36 from 59, with no material credit losses.

The inventory is mostly hardware waiting for data centers to be ready. Super Micro raised its full-year revenue outlook to $72 billion to $82 billion, from $65 billion to $72 billion, and Long said, "What governs the range is not demand, and it is not our ability to build."

Capex isn't the problem. It has stayed under $100 million a quarter for two years, while cash from operations has swung by billions:

SMCI Quarterly Operating Cash Flow vs. Capex: Dec. 2024-Sept. 2026 (TIKR)

title: Nvidia Faces “Too Many Semiconductors and Not Enough Data Center Shells” by 2028, Goldman Warns

Nvidia Faces “Too Many Semiconductors and Not Enough Data Center Shells” by 2028, Goldman Warns

Nvidia Faces "Too Many Semiconductors and Not Enough Data Center Shells" by 2028, Goldman Warns ©@NIKILAY GLUHOV from Getty Images via Canva, @Sergei Starostin from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Goldman Sachs warned that by 2028 there won't be enough data center shells for all the AI chips being made, and Super Micro Computer's CFO says shells already set the pace of its deliveries.

For NVIDIA, chips waiting on buildings would hit inventory and pricing long before any customer cancels an order.

NVIDIA's inventory more than doubled to $31.6 billion over the year to July 2026, about in step with revenue, and gross margin was 75% in the latest quarter.

NVIDIA's Nov. 17 report is the next test: inventory against revenue, and the margin guide for the January quarter.

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) had lost nearly $1.4 trillion of market value from its October record by the close on Nov. 5, after a 9% drop that day on midterm data center fears.

Now Goldman Sachs sees a problem that could hurt NVIDIA even if demand holds up.

In a note read out on CNBC's Squawk on the Street on Nov. 6, Goldman pointed to "the view that by 28 we won't have enough data center shells, that is land, power, shell and therefore will likely have too many semiconductors and not enough data center shells for them to go into."

That's a bear case even a demand bull has to take seriously.

Super Micro is already waiting on buildings

On its fiscal first-quarter call on Nov. 3, Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) raised its full-year revenue outlook to $72 billion to $82 billion, from $65 billion to $72 billion. But CFO Mark Long was clear about what sets the pace: "The binding constraints on AI build-outs across this industry right now are land, power and data center shells."

He said the range depends on "the pace at which customer facilities become ready to receive what we've already manufactured." And about $2.3 billion of the quarter's revenue was catch-up from earlier deployments, so Super Micro's results already move with its customers' buildings.

Elon Musk's list of bottlenecks is longer still. Replying on X to a post that summed up his Dwarkesh Patel interview as saying the industry would soon be "making more AI chips than we can actually turn on," Musk added: "And electrical equipment, cooling, networking and batteries."

Wall Street assumes every chip gets plugged in

Hewlett Packard Enterprise HPE trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 10.08X, below the Zacks Computer and Technology sector's P/E of 16.76X. The discounted valuation of HPE stock is further substantiated by the Zacks Value Score of A.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

The discounted valuation remains despite HPE stock climbing 98% year to date, outperforming the broader sector and the Zacks Computer - Integrated Systems industry's return of 65.2% and 4.1%, respectively.

HPE YTD Performance Chart
Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

HPE Experiences Growth Across Cloud and Networking

Hewlett Packard Enterprise operates across three primary business segments, namely Cloud & AI, Networking, and Corporate Investments and Other, serving enterprise customers with infrastructure, software, services and flexible consumption solutions. Cloud & AI combines HPE's server, storage and financial services businesses.

HPE's server portfolio includes general-purpose and workload-optimized systems, high-performance computing, supercomputing, AI infrastructure, data analytics and transaction processing. Its storage offerings include HPE Alletra, unstructured data solutions, data protection, GreenLake Flex and related software. The segment is benefiting from growing demand for AI-ready servers and enterprise infrastructure. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, Cloud & AI generated $9.04 billion in revenues, up 25.4% year over year.

HPE's networking develops and sells network and security products and services across campus, branch, data center, routing and security markets. Its portfolio includes wireless access points, switches, routers, gateways, network-management software, support and professional services. The acquisition of Juniper Networks has expanded HPE's networking capabilities and exposure to AI data center infrastructure. HPE's networking revenues reached $2.89 billion in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, rising 10% on a normalized basis.

Corporate Investments and Other includes Advisory and Professional Services, Telco, Instant On and Hewlett Packard Labs. These activities complement HPE's broader technology portfolio through consulting, specialized connectivity offerings and research. Across these businesses, HPE is also expanding GreenLake, its consumption-based hybrid cloud platform, connecting infrastructure, software and services. Together, its three segments position HPE to address demand for AI infrastructure, modern networking and hybrid cloud environments.
